title: The Value Without a Twin
statement:
You get an array nums. Every value in it appears exactly twice, except one value, which appears exactly once. The two copies of a value can be anywhere in the array, not necessarily next to each other.

Return the value that appears once.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: 7 and 2 each have a partner somewhere in the array. 9 is alone.
Negative values work the same way. XOR acts on the bit pattern, sign bit included, so no special case is needed.
The lone value can be 0, so 0 cannot double as a "not found yet" marker. It is also neither the smallest nor the largest value.

constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 100 001, and the length is odd
Exactly one value appears once; every other value appears exactly twice
hints: A map from value to count works, but uses O(n) memory. Is there an operation that makes two equal values disappear?
Look at XOR: what is x ^ x? What is x ^ 0? Does the order of XOR operations matter?
XOR every value together. Each pair cancels to 0, wherever its two copies sit, and only the lone value survives.

explain.intuition:
XOR compares two numbers bit by bit: a result bit is 1 when the two input bits differ. Three facts follow, and they carry this whole pattern:

a ^ a = 0 (every bit matches itself), a ^ 0 = a (XOR with zero changes nothing), and XOR is commutative and associative, so order does not matter. Fold the whole array with XOR and you may as well regroup it as pairs: (7 ^ 7) ^ (2 ^ 2) ^ 9 = 0 ^ 0 ^ 9 = 9. The pairs cancel out wherever they sit in the array, and the lone value is all that is left.

It is like toggling a set of feature flags: flipping the same flag twice leaves it as it was, so only flags flipped an odd number of times stay changed. Negatives need no special handling. In JavaScript the values fit in 32 bits, so ^ is exact. Python treats a negative int as an endless run of sign bits, and XOR is still exact.
steps: Start with acc = 0, since XOR with 0 changes nothing.
For each value v, set acc = acc ^ v.
Return acc. Every paired value has cancelled itself out.
pitfalls: Sorting and comparing neighbours, but only checking pairs at even positions and forgetting the lone value can be the last element.
Using a sum trick such as 2 · sum(distinct values) − sum(nums). It works, but it needs a set, so it is O(n) memory.
Starting the accumulator at nums[0] and then also XOR-ing nums[0] in the loop. That cancels the first value.

solutions.title: Count every value
solutions.idea: Count occurrences in a map, then return the value whose count is 1. Simple, but O(n) memory.

solutions.title: Sort and walk in pairs
solutions.idea: After sorting, copies sit side by side. Step two at a time; the first position whose neighbour differs holds the lone value, or it is the last element.

solutions.title: XOR everything
solutions.idea: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, in any order. XOR all values together: the pairs cancel and the lone value remains.

followups: Now every value appears three times except one. XOR no longer cancels. How can you count bits per position instead?
Two values appear once and the rest twice. The XOR of everything is a ^ b. How can one set bit of that result split the array into two groups?
